title: Moving Coil Galvanometer and Its Conversion to Ammeter/Voltmeter
subcategory: Moving Charges and Magnetism — Galvanometer, Ammeter, Voltmeter

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 12 — Moving Charges and Magnetism

summary: A galvanometer detects small currents via coil deflection in a magnetic field; converting it into an ammeter requires a LOW-resistance shunt in PARALLEL, while converting it into a voltmeter requires a HIGH-resistance multiplier in SERIES — opposite modifications for opposite purposes.
explanation: A moving coil galvanometer detects current by the torque a current-carrying coil experiences in a radial magnetic field, τ = NIAB, balanced against a restoring torque from a spring, producing an angular deflection proportional to current — but a galvanometer has significant internal (coil) resistance and can only safely handle very small currents, so it cannot be used directly to measure larger currents or voltages in a circuit without modification. To convert a galvanometer into an AMMETER (which must be connected in SERIES in a circuit and should ideally have very LOW resistance, so it doesn't significantly alter the current it's measuring), a small resistance called a SHUNT is connected in PARALLEL with the galvanometer — this shunt diverts most of the current around the galvanometer coil, letting only a small, safe fraction pass through it, while the combination's overall resistance becomes very low. To convert a galvanometer into a VOLTMETER (which must be connected in PARALLEL across the component being measured and should ideally have very HIGH resistance, so it draws negligible current from the circuit), a large resistance is connected in SERIES with the galvanometer — this increases the combination's total resistance substantially, ensuring minimal current is drawn while allowing the voltage to be calculated from the small current that does flow through the modified device. This is precisely why an ideal ammeter has ZERO resistance and an ideal voltmeter has INFINITE resistance — real devices only approximate these ideals, and inserting a real ammeter/voltmeter into a circuit always introduces a small, unavoidable measurement error by slightly changing the very current/voltage being measured.
commonMisconceptions: Mixing up the connection type for shunt vs. multiplier resistance — a shunt (for ammeter conversion) goes in PARALLEL with the galvanometer, while a multiplier (for voltmeter conversion) goes in SERIES; this reversal is one of the most common exam errors in this topic.

Believing an ammeter should have high resistance to 'accurately measure' current — the opposite is true: an ammeter must have LOW resistance so that inserting it in series doesn't significantly reduce the very current it's trying to measure.

Assuming a galvanometer can be used directly as an ammeter or voltmeter without modification — its high sensitivity to tiny currents and significant coil resistance make direct use impractical/inaccurate for measuring typical circuit currents or voltages without the shunt/multiplier conversion.
examples: A galvanometer with coil resistance 100 Ω, converted into an ammeter using a small shunt resistance of just a few ohms in parallel, so most current bypasses the galvanometer coil.

The same galvanometer converted into a voltmeter by adding a large resistance (e.g. several kilohms) in series, so it draws minimal current while still deflecting proportionally to the voltage across it.
genZNote: Ammeter: low resistance, blends into the circuit. Voltmeter: high resistance, barely interferes at all.
